603.title: The pure spring
603.hook: curse a clear spring and it keeps flowing clear (Meditations 8.51)
603.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use the spring as a picture after an insult: they let the sting register, then turn their attention back to what they meant to do anyway, and let the words settle and wash out.

segments.voice: Yesterday: George Long's translation, not the whole life at once. Your line was this piece only. Did you manage to plan only today? Day six hundred three.

A spring in the hills, the water so clear you can count the pebbles. Someone stands at the edge and shouts at it. Calls it names. Kicks dirt into it. What does the spring do? Nothing dramatic. It just keeps coming up from below, and in a minute the water's clear again. Marcus put that picture in book eight, right after imagining the worst that people could do to him. Today: the pure spring.
screen: `WATER YOU CAN COUNT PEBBLES IN.` → `SOMEONE CURSES IT.` → `THE PURE SPRING.`

segments.voice: First, the worst case. Marcus starts the entry bluntly: suppose people kill you, cut you to pieces, curse you. What can any of that do to stop your mind from staying pure, wise, sober and just? He isn't saying it wouldn't hurt. He's asking what it can reach. Second, the spring. Imagine, he says, someone standing beside a clear, sweet spring and cursing it. The spring doesn't stop sending up good water. Throw in mud, or worse, and it quickly scatters it, washes it out, and isn't stained. The spring isn't defending itself. It's simply still flowing from below, faster than the dirt can settle. Third, spring or well. Marcus then asks how you can have an ever-flowing spring inside you, and not just a well, a still pit that holds whatever is thrown into it. His answer: keep shaping yourself, hour by hour, toward freedom, with kindness, simplicity and modesty. A well depends on what reaches it. A spring has its own source. Fourth, what it isn't. This isn't pretending an insult didn't land. Even a clear spring goes cloudy for a moment. The point is what happens next: whether the mud sinks in and stays, or gets carried off by what keeps rising. Earlier in the same entry Marcus gives himself a short list: don't be sluggish in action, or muddled in conversation, or wandering in thought. The spring is that list, kept running.
screen: `WHAT CAN AN INSULT REACH?` · `CURSE A SPRING; IT KEEPS FLOWING.` · `A SPRING, NOT A WELL.` · `CLOUDY FOR A MOMENT, THEN CLEAR.` · then, large: `THE SPRING RUNS CLEAR.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one sharp thing someone said to you recently. Something small, not the worst thing. Let it land for a moment. Notice where it lands: chest, jaw, stomach. Now picture the spring. The words fall in like a handful of dirt. Don't push them out. Just feel what keeps rising underneath: your breath, your own steadiness, whatever good you meant to do today anyway. Watch the water clear, a little at a time. The bell holds the time.
Fountain. Marcus's picture: curse a clear spring, throw dirt in it, and it keeps sending up clean water that carries the dirt away. Today's word.
Your line: the spring runs clear. The next time someone's words land hard today, let them cloud you for a moment, then say the spring runs clear, and go on. Day six hundred three.

604.title: Light poured out
604.hook: sunlight seems poured down but is never used up (Meditations 8.57)
604.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus use sunlight as a daily reminder: a few minutes in the light, and then attention given to others the way it falls, steady and unforced.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fountain. Your line was the spring runs clear. When something clouded you, did the water clear? Day six hundred four.

Sit in a room with one window on a sunny afternoon and watch the patch of light on the floor. It's been pouring in all day. More light every minute, and the window never runs dry. The sun never sends a bill. Nobody has to refill it. Marcus noticed the same plain thing, sunlight coming in, and found in it a picture of how a mind should move through the world. Today: aktines.
screen: `A PATCH OF LIGHT ON THE FLOOR.` → `POURING IN ALL DAY.` → `LIGHT POURED OUT.`

segments.voice: First, the puzzle. The sun's light seems poured down, Marcus says, spread out in every direction, and yet it isn't poured away. It isn't used up. The spreading, he says, is a kind of stretching out. Second, his word game. The Greek word for rays is aktines, and Marcus says they're called that from a verb meaning to be stretched out. It's his own word play, and the point isn't the dictionary. It's the picture: light reaches out without leaving its source. Third, the beam in a dark room. Watch, he says, sunlight coming through a narrow opening into a dark house. It travels in a straight line, and when it meets something solid that blocks it, it rests there. It doesn't slide off. It doesn't fall. It just lights up what's in front of it. Fourth, the mind. That's how Marcus wants his own mind to pour itself out: not emptied, not crashing violently into whatever stands in the way, but resting on it, and lighting whatever will take the light. And if something refuses it, he says, that thing only deprives itself. So attention, warmth, effort: given like sunlight, they can reach far and still not run out, as long as they're poured, not thrown.

segments.voice: If you can, move into sunlight: a window, a doorway, a patch on the floor. If it's night, picture one. Let the light rest on your hands. Notice that it doesn't push. It doesn't rush. It just arrives and stays. Breathe. Now think of one person you'll see today, and imagine your attention reaching them like that: steady, warm, not forcing, not running out. The bell holds the time.
Aktines. Marcus's Greek word for the sun's rays: stretched out in every direction, never used up, resting on what they meet. Today's word.

605.title: Teach or bear with them
605.hook: people exist for one another: teach them, or bear with them (Meditations 8.59)
605.howItsDone: People who live by this line of Marcus often make the choice consciously when someone frustrates them: either explain once, kindly, or let it go without resentment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: aktines. Your line was poured out. Whom did your attention reach today, and did it run out? Day six hundred five.

Somebody at work does it wrong again. The same report, the same mistake, the same cheerful shrug. You have a few options. Explain it, one more time. Let it go. Or the third thing, the one that tends to happen without anyone deciding on it: stew, complain about them to someone else, and slowly come to dislike them. Marcus has an entry in book eight that's only two short sentences long, and it leaves that third option out. Today: the third door.
screen: `THE SAME MISTAKE AGAIN.` → `THREE OPTIONS.` → `TEACH OR BEAR WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: First, the line, in George Long's 1862 translation: “Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then or bear with them.” That's the whole entry. Second, the reason comes first. Before the advice, Marcus lays the ground under it: people are for each other. The idea comes back again and again in the Meditations. We're made to work together, like hands, or feet, or eyelids, or the rows of upper and lower teeth, an image he used back in book two. If that's true, then the person who frustrates you is still someone you exist for. Third, two doors. If you can show them a better way, teach. Not lecture, not win: teach, which means you actually want them to understand. And if you can't, because they won't listen, or it isn't your place, or you've already tried, then bear with them. Put up with them. Carry it. Fourth, the missing door. Notice what isn't on the list: resent them, gossip about them, write them off. Marcus doesn't argue against those here. He just doesn't offer them. This note quietly shuts that third door. And it works in both directions. Somewhere, someone is deciding right now whether to teach you or bear with you.
screen: `MEN EXIST FOR ONE ANOTHER.` · `MADE TO WORK TOGETHER.` · `DOOR ONE: TEACH. DOOR TWO: BEAR.` · `NO THIRD DOOR.` · then, large: `TEACH OR BEAR.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one person who frustrates you, in a small, ordinary way. Picture the thing they do. Now ask honestly: is this something I can teach? Is there a kind, clear way to show them, one they could actually hear? If yes, picture saying it, gently, once. If no, picture bearing it: letting it pass through you without the stewing. Choose one door for this person. Breathe with that choice. The bell holds the time.
Third door. The one option Marcus leaves off his list when he says teach them or bear with them: resent, gossip, write them off. Today's word.
Your line: teach or bear. Today, teach one person something kindly, or bear with one person quietly. Skip the third door. Day six hundred five.

606.title: For one another
606.hook: nature made us for one another, so wronging others wrongs the whole (Meditations 9.1)
606.tomorrow: Death as a work of nature
606.howItsDone: Readers who take this passage to heart often treat small wrongs as worth fixing even when no one would notice: returning the extra change, correcting the excuse, giving the credit back.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the third door. Your line was teach or bear. Which door did you choose, and with whom? Day six hundred six.

A cashier gives you too much change. Ten dollars, maybe. Nobody saw. The store is big; it'll never notice. There may be a small tug anyway, even if it's hard to say why. Book nine of the Meditations opens with Marcus's answer, and it's bigger than ten dollars. He says a wrong like that isn't only against the cashier. It's against the whole. Today, as book nine begins: pulled thread.

First, the claim. Marcus opens book nine with a startling sentence: whoever acts unjustly acts impiously. A wrong done to a person is also a wrong against the order of things itself. Second, the reason. Nature, he says, made rational beings for one another, to help each other as each deserves, and never to harm. So when you harm someone, you're not just breaking a rule. You're working against what you were made for, and against the nature of the whole, which Marcus here calls the most ancient of divinities. Third, the stretch. He doesn't stop at cheating. Lying, he says, is impiety too, because the nature of the whole is truth, and the liar sets himself at odds with it, whether on purpose or carelessly. Even being thrown around by pleasure and pain, he says, ends up unjust, because it makes us unfair in how we treat people and things. Fourth, how far it reaches. Marcus's view rests on nature and the gods, and not everyone shares it. But his picture is easy to test on an ordinary day. The extra ten dollars, the excuse that wasn't true, the credit taken for someone else's work: on his view, none of them stays in its box, because the box was never separate. For Marcus we're one fabric, and a pulled thread puckers the whole cloth.
screen: `INJUSTICE IS IMPIETY.` · `MADE TO HELP, NEVER TO HARM.` · `LYING, TOO, IS AT ODDS WITH THE WHOLE.` · `SMALL WRONGS LEAK.` · then, large: `FOR ONE ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last few days for one small wrong you did. Nothing dramatic: a sharp word, a corner cut, a promise that slid, change you didn't hand back. Don't punish yourself. Just find it. Now picture the smallest way to set it right: a message, an apology, a returned thing, a task redone. See yourself doing it. Picture the thread pulling straight. The bell holds the time.
Pulled thread. Marcus's image for one wrong done: it puckers the whole cloth we're woven into. Today's word.
Your line: we're one fabric. Right one small wrong today, however small. Notice how the whole feels afterward. Day six hundred six.

607.title: Death as a work of nature
607.hook: death is like teething, growing up, having children: one of nature's works (Meditations 9.3)
607.howItsDone: Stoic readers often reflect briefly on mortality as part of nature's ordinary course, alongside growing up and growing old, as a way of meeting it calmly rather than with dread.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pulled thread, and one small wrong set right. Your line was we're one fabric. Did you pull a thread straight? Day six hundred seven.

A baby is cutting teeth: fussy, drooling, awake at three in the morning. Nobody calls it a tragedy. It's hard, it hurts, and everyone in the house knows it's just what babies do on the way to growing up. Marcus picks up exactly that ordinary picture, teething, and sets it beside something we usually treat very differently. Gently, because it's a tender subject, today we read his thought on dying. Today: cutting teeth.
screen: `A BABY CUTTING TEETH.` → `HARD, BUT NATURAL.` → `DEATH AS A WORK OF NATURE.`

segments.voice: First, the list. In book nine Marcus writes: don't despise death, but be content with it, since it's one of the things nature wills. Then he names the others. Being young and growing old. Growing up and reaching full size. Getting teeth, a beard, gray hair. Conceiving, carrying a child, giving birth. All the works our seasons of life bring. Dying, he says, belongs on the same list. Second, the pace. He doesn't say rush toward it, and he doesn't say ignore it. He says wait for it the way you'd wait for a child to be born: not anxious, not careless, knowing it comes in its own time. That, he says, is how a thoughtful person meets it. Third, a plainer comfort. Then Marcus does something surprising. He offers a homelier consolation, the kind that reaches the heart: think of the things you'll leave, and the habits of the people you'll no longer have to live among. But in the same breath he checks himself. Don't be offended with them, he writes. Care for them, and bear with them gently. Fourth, what this is and isn't. This is a Stoic view, and not everyone holds it. Many traditions speak of death in terms of a soul, a judgment, a world to come, or rebirth, and Marcus himself, across the book, is unsure what follows. What he offers here isn't a teaching about the afterlife. It's a posture: to see dying as part of the same nature that brought teeth and gray hair, and so not to meet it with horror.
screen: `TEETH, GRAY HAIR, BIRTH, DEATH.` · `WAIT AS FOR A BIRTH.` · `A HOMELIER COMFORT, CHECKED.` · `A POSTURE, NOT A DOCTRINE.` · then, large: `NATURE'S WORK.`

segments.voice: This one is gentle. Settle, and breathe. If this subject is tender for you right now, simply rest with the breath; that's enough. Otherwise, bring to mind the changes your body has already lived through: first teeth, a growth spurt, a first gray hair, maybe a pregnancy or a child. Each one arrived on its own schedule. Let the thought sit quietly beside them: my life has a shape, and an ending is part of the shape. Don't push it. Just breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Cutting teeth. Marcus sets dying beside this, and growing old, and gray hair: just one more of nature's works, waited for, not dreaded. Today's word.
Your line: nature's work. When you notice something changing in your body today, a gray hair, a stiff knee, say nature's work, and let it be ordinary. Day six hundred seven.

608.title: The wrongdoer wrongs himself
608.hook: whoever does wrong, wrongs himself first (Meditations 9.4)
608.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use this line to turn anger toward someone who wronged them into something closer to pity, while still acting to protect themselves and others.

segments.voice: Yesterday: cutting teeth, as ordinary as teeth and gray hair. Your line was nature's work. What did you let be ordinary? Day six hundred eight.

Someone cuts you off in traffic, then makes a rude gesture for good measure. In the moment there's only one victim, and it's you. But follow that driver home. The rest of their evening is still inside that anger. Their shoulders are still up. Their day is still a little worse for it. Marcus wrote a very short entry in book nine about exactly this, two lines long. Today: the wrongdoer wrongs himself.
screen: `CUT OFF IN TRAFFIC.` → `FOLLOW THEM HOME.` → `THE WRONGDOER WRONGS HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the line, in George Long's 1862 translation: “He who does wrong does wrong against himself.” Then Marcus adds: whoever acts unjustly acts unjustly toward himself, because he makes himself bad. Second, what's being harmed. For Marcus, the only real harm is harm to your character, the ruling part of you. Your car, your schedule, even your body can be damaged by someone else. Your goodness can be damaged only by you. So the person who wrongs you has, at most, dented your fender. They've dented their own self. Third, where that leads. If that's true, the wrongdoer isn't someone to hate. They're someone to pity, the way you'd pity a person who stepped on their own foot and then blamed the floor. That isn't looking down on them. It's seeing the injury clearly. Fourth, the line after. The very next entry adds a twist that keeps this honest: a person can act unjustly by not doing something, too. So pity is no reason to stand by. Standing by can be a wrong of its own. What shifts is the feeling underneath. Not, how dare they. Rather, what did that cost them? And by Marcus's logic it cuts close to home: every time we snap, cheat, or lie, the first person changed is the one who did it.

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who wronged you: a small or middle-sized wrong, not your deepest wound. Picture what they did. Now picture them afterward: the evening that followed, what they had to tell themselves, what kind of person that act made them a little more of. See if you can feel something besides anger. Maybe a sliver of pity. It doesn't excuse them. It just sees them. The bell holds the time.
George Long, whose translation gives Marcus's short entry: he who does wrong does wrong against himself, and makes himself worse. Today's word.

609.title: Enough for now
609.hook: a present judgment, a present act, a present acceptance: that's enough (Meditations 9.6)
609.howItsDone: Some readers of the Meditations use this entry as a short evening check: did I see truly, act for others, and accept what came today? If so, the day was enough.

segments.voice: Yesterday: George Long's wrongdoer, who wrongs himself. Your line was he's hurt himself. Did the anger turn into anything else? Day six hundred nine, the end of a week.

Your phone shows you a hundred things you could want. A better kitchen, a different job, a calmer family, the trip, the body, the version of you that's on top of everything. The list never ends because it isn't built to end. Then, in book nine, Marcus writes an entry only one sentence long, and in George Long's English it finishes on a word that list never says. Enough. Today: three presents.
screen: `A HUNDRED THINGS TO WANT.` → `A LIST BUILT NOT TO END.` → `ENOUGH FOR NOW.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. Marcus writes, roughly: your present judgment, grasping things as they are; your present action, done for the common good; your present acceptance of whatever comes from outside you. These are enough. Second, three presents. Look at the parts. A judgment: seeing this moment truly. An action: doing this moment's work for others. An acceptance: being at peace with what this moment brought. Each one happens now. None of them needs a future that hasn't arrived. Third, why enough is radical. So much of what drives us says not yet. Not until the promotion, the cure, the apology. Marcus says the three things a good life needs are all available in the present, and that's sufficient. Not perfect. Sufficient. The Greek verb behind that word means it suffices. Fourth, the week, looking back. The spring runs clear. Poured out. Teach or bear. We're one fabric. Nature's work. He's hurt himself. And now, it suffices. Seven entries, and every one pulls the same way: away from what other people do and what tomorrow might bring, toward what you can see, do and accept right here. Across books eight and nine, the lesson keeps coming back to the same small size: this moment, and three things you can do in it.
screen: `JUDGMENT, ACTION, ACCEPTANCE.` · `ALL THREE HAPPEN NOW.` · `NOT PERFECT. SUFFICIENT.` · `A WEEK OF WHAT'S HERE.` · then, large: `IT SUFFICES.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Name one thing about this exact moment you've been fighting: the noise, the tiredness, the weather, the thing that didn't happen today. Don't pretend you like it. Just accept that it's here. Say inside, this is what's here. Then check the three. Am I seeing this moment truly? Is there something good I can do in it? Can I accept what it brought? If you can answer, that's enough. The bell holds the time.
Three presents. Marcus's list: a true judgment, an action for the common good, an acceptance of what comes. They suffice. Today's word.
Your line: it suffices. When the list of wants starts up today, name the three presents, and say your line. Day six hundred nine.
